nuance: 평일 is Sino-Korean 平日 (平 'flat/ordinary' + 日 'day'), literally an 'ordinary day' — Monday through Friday, the regular working days, set against 주말 (weekend) and 휴일 (holiday/day off). The dividing line vs 주중 (週中, 'inside the week'): 평일 simply names the ordinary days as a category, while 주중 frames those same days as the span 'during the week' and pairs naturally with 주말 as a matched contrast (주중에는 바쁘고 주말에는 쉬어요). 평일 is neutral and used by everyone in any register, from a weather report to a friend's text. It habitually appears as 평일 + time-of-day (평일 아침/낮/저녁) and with 에/에는. The English-speaker pitfall: 'weekday' in English can mean 'any single working day' OR the whole work portion of the week, but in Korean 평일 leans toward the category of ordinary days, so for a duration like 'during the week I'm busy' Koreans more often say 주중에는 바빠요; also don't write the near-homophone 휴일 (rest day) by mistake.

nuance: 주중 is Sino-Korean 週中 (週 'week' + 中 'middle/inside'), literally 'inside the week' — the Monday-to-Friday stretch viewed as a span of time. It overlaps heavily with 평일 (平日), but the dividing line is framing: 평일 names the ordinary days as a category, whereas 주중 emphasizes the duration 'during the week' and is the natural partner of 주말 (週末, 'week-end') in a balanced contrast — Koreans reflexively say 주중에는 ... 주말에는 .... Register is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 에/에는, with 내내 ('주중 내내', all week long), and with verbs of routine (일하다, 바쁘다). The English-speaker pitfall: 'midweek' in English often means specifically Tuesday–Thursday, but 주중 covers the whole working span, so don't narrow it to just the middle days; and because 주중 is a time-span noun it still needs 에 (주중에 바빠요), unlike a bare adverb.

I exercise every week.

nuance: 매주 is Sino-Korean 每週 (每 'each/every' + 週 'week'), literally 'each week' — every week without exception. The 每 prefix is the same building block in 매일 (every day), 매달/매월 (every month), 매년 (every year), so learning it once unlocks the whole set. Unlike a time-point noun, 매주 behaves as a frequency adverb and normally takes NO particle, sitting just before the verb (매주 만나요), though you can add 마다 for emphasis (매주마다). It collocates with a following day (매주 금요일), with counts (매주 두 번), and with 꼬박꼬박/규칙적으로 for 'regularly'. The English-speaker pitfall: learners copy the 'on weekdays → 평일에' habit and wrongly stick 에 onto 매주 (✗매주에); 매주 is already adverbial, so 매주 가요 is complete. Also distinguish 매주 (every week, recurring) from 이번 주 (this week, one specific week) — different concept entirely.

usage: 초 = beginning; 매달 초에 월급을 받아요
말 = end; 매달 말에 정산해요 = settle up at month-end

I buy books every month.

nuance: 매달 is a hybrid: 매(每, Sino 'every') + 달 (native Korean 'month/moon'), literally 'every month'. Its fully Sino twin 매월 (每月) means the same and is interchangeable, though 매월 feels a touch more formal/written (notices, contracts) while 매달 is the warmer spoken choice. Like all 매- words it works as a frequency adverb and takes NO particle (매달 내요), optionally 매달마다 for emphasis. It collocates heavily with money life — 월급(salary), 방세/월세(rent), 저금/적금(savings), 공과금(utility bills) — and with 초/말 (start/end of month). The English-speaker pitfall: don't fuse 월 and 일 into ✗매월일; and keep 매달 (every month, recurring) separate from 한 달 (one month, a single month's duration: 한 달 동안 = for a month). Because 달 also means 'moon', context disambiguates, but in time contexts 매달 is unambiguously 'monthly'.

nuance: 매년 is Sino-Korean 每年 (每 'every' + 年 'year'), literally 'each year' — every year without exception, the time-axis sibling of 매일/매주/매달. It functions as a frequency adverb and takes NO particle (매년 가요). Its near-synonym 해마다 (해 = native 'year' + 마다 'each') means exactly the same and is slightly warmer/more spoken; both are correct, so 매년 여행해요 = 해마다 여행해요. 매년 collocates with seasons (매년 봄/겨울), recurring events (매년 생일/명절/시험), and 초/말 (year's start/end). The English-speaker pitfall: pronunciation — 매년 is [매년], NOT [메년]; the vowel ㅐ should not collapse to ㅔ in careful speech. Also keep 매년 (every year, recurring) distinct from 작년 (last year) and 내년 (next year), which are single specific years, and from 일 년 (one year's duration: 일 년 동안 = for one year).

usage: 만 = 'only'; 오 분만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just five minutes

examples: 십 분 남았어요.
Ten minutes are left.

세 시 삼십 분에 만나요.
Let's meet at 3:30.
Mixed clock: native 세 시 (3 o'clock) + Sino 삼십 분 (30 min)
nuance: 분 is the time unit 'minute', written with the hanja 分 (to divide/a part) — a minute being a division of the hour. The crucial rule: 분 ALWAYS takes Sino-Korean numbers (일·이·삼·사·오·...), so it's 오 분, 삼십 분, never the native 하나·둘·셋. This creates Korea's famous mixed clock, where the HOUR uses native numbers + 시 (한 시, 두 시) but the MINUTE uses Sino numbers + 분 (십 분, 삼십 분): 한 시 십 분 = 1:10. Note 분 also means 'a respected person' (한 분 = one person, honorific) and is the honorific counter for people — same syllable, totally different word, disambiguated by context. The English-speaker pitfall: applying the native numbers used for 시 to 분 as well (✗한 분 for one minute — that actually means 'one person, honorific'); the correct 'one minute' is 일 분. Collocates with 후/전 (after/before), 동안 (for), 정도 (about), 만 (only), and 걸리다 (to take).

nuance: 초 is the time unit 'second', from the hanja 秒 (a tiny fraction of time). Like 분 (minute), it ALWAYS takes Sino-Korean numbers (일·이·삼·...), so it's 십 초, 삼십 초, never native 열·서른. It most often appears alongside 분 to give a precise duration (삼 분 삼십 초 = 3:30 of cooking time, lap times, countdowns) and with 동안 (for), 안에 (within), 후/전 (after/before). Beware: the syllable 초 is a homonym jungle — 초 also means 'candle' (촛불 = candlelight), 'vinegar' (식초), and 'the beginning of' a period (월초 = early month, 초반 = early stage); only context tells them apart. The English-speaker pitfall: again, do not import native numbers (✗열 초); and don't confuse the duration 초 (second) with 첫/처음 (first/at first) — 'the first second' is 첫 일 초, while 처음 means 'at first' in a sequence. For everyday speech Koreans round to 분 and rarely specify 초 except in cooking, sports, or countdowns.

nuance: 시각 is Sino-Korean 時刻 (時 'time' + 刻 'a carved mark/notch') — literally a 'carved mark of time', i.e. one precise point on the clock, like a departure, arrival, or boarding moment. The all-important contrast is with its near-twin 시간 時間 (時 'time' + 間 'interval/space'): 시각 = a single instant ('at what moment'), whereas 시간 = a span/duration OR the general notion of 'time/hours' ('how long'). So 출발 시각 = the departure moment (e.g. 3:00), but 비행 시간 = the flight duration (e.g. 2 hours). 시각 carries a formal, schedule-board, announcement flavor — you meet it on tickets, timetables, and in news ('현재 시각'), but in casual chat people just say 시간 even for a point in time (몇 시에 만나? rather than 몇 시각에). The English-speaker pitfall: 'time' in English covers both, so learners reach for the familiar 시간 everywhere and never use 시각, or worse, swap them — saying ✗시각이 없어요 for 'I have no time' (that should be 시간이 없어요, a duration). Use 시각 only when you mean a pinpoint moment, usually formal.

usage: 시험 기간이 길어요 = the exam period is long
방학 기간에 여행해요 = travel during the break
계약 기간은 일 년이에요 = the term is one year
할인 기간을 놓쳤어요 = I missed the sale window
examples: 접수 기간이 끝났어요.
The application period ended.
Official-notice tone; 접수 = receiving applications
짧은 기간에 많이 배웠어요.
I learned a lot in a short period.
짧다 → 짧은; 기간 takes 에 to mean 'within that span'
공사 기간 동안 길이 막혀요.
The road is blocked during the construction period.
기간 동안 = 'for the duration of'; everyday signage Korean
nuance: 기간 is Sino-Korean 期間 (期 'a fixed term/appointed time' + 間 'interval') — a defined stretch of time with a clear START and END, such as an exam season, a vacation, a contract term, or a sale window. Contrast it sharply with 시간 時間: 시간 is generic 'time/hours/duration' you measure (세 시간 = three hours), while 기간 is a bounded named span you don't usually count in hours (시험 기간 = the exam period, not '×N hours'). Also distinguish 동안, which is the grammatical word for 'during/for' and attaches to spans (방학 동안), whereas 기간 is the noun naming the span itself (often combined: 방학 기간 동안). 기간 collocates with administrative life — 접수/신청 기간 (application period), 계약/임대 기간 (contract/lease term), 유효 기간 (validity period/expiry), 공사 기간 — and takes 에 ('within') or 동안 ('throughout'). The English-speaker pitfall: translating every 'time' as 시간 and saying ✗시험 시간이 길어요 to mean 'the exam season is long' — that actually reads as 'the exam's duration (one sitting) is long'; the season is 시험 기간.

usage: 최근에 이사했어요 = I moved recently — 에 needed for the time point
As a modifier, 최근 attaches directly: 최근 뉴스를 봤어요
까지 = 'up to'; 최근까지 일했어요 = worked until lately
Set phrase 들어 = 'entering into'; 최근 들어 부쩍 추워졌어요
examples: 최근에 책을 많이 읽어요.
I've been reading a lot of books lately.
최근에 + present = an ongoing recent habit
최근에 친구를 만났어요.
I met a friend recently.
With past tense, 최근에 marks a recent completed event
최근 몇 년 동안 많이 변했어요.
It has changed a lot over the past few years.
최근 + 몇 년 동안 = 'over the recent few years', written/formal feel
nuance: 최근 is Sino-Korean 最近 (最 'most' + 近 'near') — literally 'most near (in time)', i.e. the recent stretch right up to now. Its near-synonym 요즘 (native, 'these days') overlaps but differs in register and shape: 최근 is more written/formal and works both as a noun-modifier (최근 동향 = recent trends) and, with 에, as a time adverb (최근에 = recently); 요즘 is purely casual-spoken and adverbial (요즘 바빠요), never a noun-modifier (✗요즘 뉴스 sounds off; 최근 뉴스 is right). A subtle nuance gap: 최근 can point to a recent completed event (최근에 갔어요 = I went recently), while 요즘 leans toward the ongoing present situation (요즘 가요 ≈ I go these days). 최근 collocates with 에, 까지, 들어, and number spans (최근 3년/몇 달). The English-speaker pitfall: 'recently' is a bare adverb in English, so learners drop the particle and say ✗최근 갔어요; as a time-point noun 최근 needs 최근에 갔어요. Conversely, when modifying a noun, you DON'T add 에 (최근 소식, not ✗최근에 소식).

usage: Stock friendly opener — no particle on 요즘
들어 = 'coming into'; 요즘 들어 자주 피곤해요 = tired often lately
요즘 같은 시대에 = 'in an age like today's'
요즘 유행이에요 = it's trendy these days (spoken)
examples: 요즘 바빠요?
Are you busy these days?
요즘 needs no particle; it works straight as an adverb
요즘 잠을 잘 못 자요.
I haven't been sleeping well lately.
못 자다 = can't sleep; 요즘 frames an ongoing present state
요즘 뭐 하고 지내요?
What have you been up to these days?
지내다 = to get along/spend one's days — warm small-talk Korean
nuance: 요즘 is a native Korean word (a contraction of 요사이 → 요즈음 → 요즘) meaning 'around now, these days, lately'. It is one of the single most common small-talk openers in Korean, the natural lead-in to 'how have you been?' Its near-synonym 최근(에) (最近, Sino 'most near') means roughly the same time but differs in register and grammar: 요즘 is warm, casual, spoken, strictly adverbial (요즘 바빠요) and CANNOT modify a noun (✗요즘 소식 → use 최근 소식); 최근 is more formal/written and can both modify nouns and, with 에, act as an adverb. Crucially 요즘 takes NO particle — it stands alone before the clause (요즘 어때요?). It pairs with 들어 ('요즘 들어' = of late), with present-tense verbs for ongoing situations, and with 같은 ('요즘 같은' = like nowadays). The English-speaker pitfall: treating 요즘 like a past-time word and saying ✗요즘 갔어요 ('I went these days'?) — 요즘 describes the ongoing present, so use present tense (요즘 가요 / 요즘 다녀요); for a finished recent event switch to 최근에 갔어요.

usage: 예전에 여기 살았어요 = I used to live here
부터 = 'from/since'; 예전부터 알았어요 = I've known since long ago
보다 = 'than'; 예전보다 좋아졌어요 = better than before
예전 모습 그대로예요 = just like you used to be
examples: 예전에는 시간이 많았어요.
In the past I had lots of time.
에는 (에+는) adds 'as for back then', contrasting with now
예전 친구를 다시 만났어요.
I met an old friend again.
예전 modifies 친구 directly — an old/former friend
예전만큼 자주 못 봐요.
We don't see each other as often as we used to.
예전만큼 = 'as much as before'; nostalgic, real-life tone
nuance: 예전 means 'the (fairly distant) past, the old days, a while back' and carries a gently nostalgic flavor, the feeling of looking back on how things used to be. Its near-synonyms map onto a distance scale: 옛날 (옛날, native 'olden times') is the most remote — fairy-tale 'once upon a time' (옛날 옛적에) or 'the old days' long gone; 예전 is past but within a person's own lived memory ('back when I was younger'); 최근 (最近) is the recent past close to now. So you'd say 예전에 여기 살았어요 (I used to live here, a few years back) but 옛날 사람들 for 'people of old'. 예전 works both as a time adverb with 에 (예전에) and as a noun-modifier (예전 사진 = old photos), and it loves 부터 (since), 보다/만큼 (than/as much as), and 그대로 (just as it was). The English-speaker pitfall: using 예전 for 'a moment ago / just now' — that's 아까 or 방금, not 예전; 예전 implies a meaningful gap of time, often months or years, viewed with hindsight, not 'earlier today'.
